who: Latin American historian at Wayne State University, 1947–1980; PhD in history, University of California, Berkeley.

evidence.says: The obituary identifies C. Norman Guice as a Latin American historian with a Berkeley history doctorate, who joined Wayne State in 1947 and retired in 1980.
Wayne State’s oral-history collection identifies Dr. C. Norman Guice as a retired history professor researching Mexican commercial and economic history.
LC identifies C. Norman Guice through Crónicas de la guerra con Chile (1881–1883) and the National Directory of Latin Americanists.

notes: Name, field, Berkeley doctorate and Wayne State service spanning all three students agree. The doctorate year was not independently verified.

who: Medieval historian at Wayne State University; author of The Arnolfini Betrothal and Sweynheym & Pannartz and the Origins of Printing in Italy.

evidence.says: The UC Press book’s 1994 author biography identifies Edwin Hall as a Wayne State history professor and author of Sweynheym & Pannartz and the Origins of Printing in Italy (1991).
The publisher attributes The Arnolfini Betrothal: Medieval Marriage and the Enigma of Van Eyck’s Double Portrait to Edwin Hall.
LC identifies this Edwin Hall through both Sweynheym & Pannartz and the Origins of Printing in Italy and The Arnolfini Betrothal.

notes: The exact books connect the authority record to the Wayne State professor; the medieval field agrees with the students’ topics. Wisconsin 1955 was not independently verified.

who: Historian of diplomatic history and East Asia at West Virginia University, 1968–2016; PhD Virginia, 1970.

evidence.says: WVU lists his faculty appointments from 1968 through 2016, a Virginia PhD in 1970, teaching in modern Japan and China, and Spoilsmen in a "Flowery Fairyland" (1998).
LC identifies Jack L. (Leonard) Hammersmith as the author of Spoilsmen in a "Flowery Fairyland" (1998).

notes: The book establishes candidate identity; employer, period, field and exact doctorate agree.

who: Charles James (Jim) Haug, historian of modern France and science and technology at Mississippi State, 1976–2004; PhD Kansas.

evidence.says: The Starkville Daily News obituary states that Charles James Haug obtained his Kansas PhD, joined Mississippi State’s history department in 1976, retired in 2004, and wrote Leisure and Urbanism about nineteenth-century Nice.
LC identifies C. James Haug as the author of Leisure & urbanism in nineteenth-century Nice (1982).
A separate LC heading for Charles James Haug cites Urban development ... (1976).

notes: The exact book links n81100747 to the Mississippi State professor; Kansas and service dates agree. n87133589 appears to be an additional authority for the same historian, but its dissertation citation was not independently reconciled.

who: Robert J. Haws, historian of U.S. legal and constitutional history at the University of Mississippi; doctorate Nebraska.

evidence.says: The university foundation identifies Robert J. Haws as a history faculty member from 1969, retiring in 2011, with undergraduate and graduate degrees from Nebraska and a specialty in U.S. legal and constitutional history.
The university’s symposium history names Robert Haws as organizer and Robert J. Haws as editor of The South’s Role in the Creation of the Bill of Rights (1991).
LC’s Robert J. Haws record cites the Bill of Rights volume and The Age of Segregation, the latter under the name Robert Haws.

notes: Full name, institution, career period, Nebraska degree and publication agree. The doctorate year was not independently verified.

who: William Anthony Hay, historian of Britain and the Atlantic world, formerly at Mississippi State; PhD Virginia, 2000.

evidence.says: Mississippi State identifies William Anthony Hay as a history faculty member since 2003, holding a Virginia doctorate and authoring The Whig Revival, 1808–1830.
The university identifies Hay as a history professor and dates his Virginia PhD to 2000, in European and international history.
LC identifies William Anthony Hay through The Whig Revival, 1808–1830.

notes: The exact book establishes candidate identity; employer, field and exact doctorate agree.

who: Judith A. Houck, historian of science, medicine and women’s health at Wisconsin–Madison; PhD there, 1998.

evidence.says: The department lists Judith A. Houck as professor of history of science, with a Wisconsin–Madison PhD in history of science and medicine in 1998; lists Hot and Bothered among her books and Suzanna Schulert among her advisees.
The catalogue attributes Common Experiences and Changing Meanings to Judith A. (Judith Anne) Houck and records it as a Madison doctoral dissertation, 1998.
LC connects Judith A. (Judith Anne) Houck with Common Experiences and Changing Meanings and Hot and Bothered.

notes: Exact doctorate, institution, dissertation, book and a named advisee connect the supervisor to the authority record.

who: Elizabeth K. Hudson, emerita history faculty at West Virginia University, with an Indiana University doctorate.

evidence.says: WVU’s history catalogue lists Elizabeth K. Hudson among emeriti faculty, with a PhD from Indiana University.
This Elizabeth Hudson authority identifies the editor of Verdi’s Il corsaro, with a variant Elisabeth Hudson.
Elizabeth Gray Hudson’s authority cites In One Place (1981), without a university affiliation or doctorate.
Elizabeth A. Hudson’s authority cites Libraries for a Lifetime (1989), without a university affiliation or doctorate.

notes: The supervisor’s institution and doctoral school are corroborated, but no supplied authority was reliably connected to her. Several records concern plainly different works or careers; the sparse remaining records do not support a definitive exclusion of every candidate.
